title: The Lesson I Learned From Jairus
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Jairus
When Faith Is Running Out, Jesus Is Just Getting Started
There are moments in life when desperation strips away every title, every achievement, every illusion of control.
Moments when the things that once made us feel important suddenly become meaningless.
Moments when all that remains is a trembling heart, a silent prayer, and a desperate hope that God still sees us.
That is where we meet Jairus.
Not as a famous synagogue ruler.
Not as a respected religious leader.
Not as a man admired by his community.
We meet him as a father.
A father watching his little girl slip away.
And if you've ever watched a dream die, a marriage crumble, a child suffer, a diagnosis arrive, a friendship collapse, or a prayer seem unanswered, then you already know something about Jairus.
His story is not merely ancient history.
His story is our story.
And hidden within it is one of the most powerful lessons about faith, surrender, and the heart of Jesus Christ.
The account is found in Mark 5:21–43, Matthew 9:18–26, and Luke 8:40–56.
Mark records that Jairus fell at Jesus' feet and pleaded earnestly for his daughter.
The Greek text says:
"παρακαλεῖ αὐτὸν πολλὰ" (parakalei auton polla)
Literally:
"He begged Him intensely."
This was not a polished prayer.
This was not a theological discussion.
This was a broken father pouring out his soul.
The man who spent years teaching others suddenly found himself unable to save the person he loved most.
And isn't that where God often meets us?
Not in our strength.
But in our surrender.
Not when we have answers.
But when we finally admit we don't.
Jairus had status.
Jesus wanted his heart.
Because God has never been impressed by our titles.
He has always been moved by our dependence.
The first lesson Jairus teaches us is this:
Faith begins where self-sufficiency ends.
Many people want Jesus as an assistant.
Jairus needed Him as a Savior.
There is a difference.
When life is comfortable, we often pray casually.
When life falls apart, we pray honestly.
And honest prayers move heaven.
As Jairus and Jesus began walking toward the house, something unexpected happened.
A woman who had suffered twelve years with a flow of blood pushed through the crowd and touched Jesus' garment.
Everything stopped.
Jesus paused.
He turned.
He spoke with her.
He healed her.
Meanwhile, Jairus waited.
Every second mattered.
Every moment felt unbearable.
His daughter was dying.
Can you imagine standing there?
Watching Jesus stop for someone else while your miracle seems to be slipping away?
Many believers know exactly what that feels like.
You pray.
Someone else gets the breakthrough.
You wait.
Someone else gets the answer.
You cry.
Someone else receives the blessing.
And suddenly your faith enters its greatest battle.
Not against circumstances.
Against discouragement.
Because waiting often feels like abandonment.
Yet God's delays are never God's denials.
While Jairus stood there watching Jesus minister to another person, heaven was accomplishing something deeper than he could understand.
The interruption was not an obstacle.
It was part of the miracle.
And perhaps that is what some readers need to hear today.
The delay you're frustrated by may actually be part of God's preparation.
The closed door.
The unanswered prayer.
The waiting season.
The silence.
It may not mean Jesus has forgotten you.
It may mean He is writing a story larger than you can currently see.
Then came the devastating news.
Messengers arrived.
They said:
"Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?"
Those words must have shattered Jairus.
The situation had moved beyond hopeless.
The opportunity seemed gone.
The prayer appeared too late.
The dream was buried.
The relationship was dead.
The future was over.
At least that's how it looked.
But then Jesus spoke one of the most beautiful statements in all Scripture.
In Greek:

"Μὴ φοβοῦ, μόνον πίστευε."
(Mē phobou, monon pisteue.)
A faithful translation:
"Do not fear. Only believe."
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not explain everything.
He did not reveal the plan.
He did not answer every question.
He simply called Jairus to trust Him.
Sometimes God gives explanations.
Sometimes He gives Himself.
And His presence is always enough.
The greatest enemy of faith is not uncertainty.
It is fear.
Fear says it is over.
Faith says Jesus has not spoken the final word.
Fear looks at circumstances.
Faith looks at Christ.
Fear magnifies impossibilities.
Faith magnifies God.
When they arrived at the house, mourners were already weeping.
The funeral atmosphere had begun.
Everyone believed the story was finished.
Everyone except Jesus.
Then Jesus said something that sounded ridiculous to everyone present.
"The child is not dead but sleeping."
The crowd laughed.
Mocked.
Dismissed Him.
Why?
Because human eyes can only see what is visible.
Jesus sees what is possible.
The same Lord who created life was standing inside the room.
Death was not intimidating Him.
The One who formed Adam from dust was not concerned about restoring breath to a little girl.
The same remains true today.
There is no dead marriage He cannot revive.
No broken heart He cannot heal.
No addicted life He cannot restore.
No prodigal child He cannot reach.
No shattered future He cannot redeem.
No scandal beyond His grace.
No failure beyond His mercy.
No sinner beyond His forgiveness.
Then comes one of the most powerful moments in the Gospels.
Jesus took the little girl by the hand.
Mark preserves the original Aramaic words:

"Talitha koum."
(ܛܠܝܬܐ ܩܘܡܝ)
A careful translation is:
"Little girl, I say to you, arise."
The detail is breathtaking.
Jesus could have simply commanded from across the room.
Instead, He touched her.
The Savior who rules galaxies reached down to hold the hand of a little girl.
That is the heart of Christ.
He is majestic enough to command heaven.
Yet compassionate enough to hold trembling hands.
And immediately she stood up.
The impossible became possible.
Death became life.
Mourning became joy.
Despair became celebration.
The story everyone thought was over became a testimony.
Because Jesus specializes in rewriting endings.
That is the lesson Jairus teaches us.
Faith is not believing God will do exactly what we want.
Faith is believing Jesus remains trustworthy even when everything appears lost.
Jairus thought Jesus needed to arrive before death.
Jesus revealed His authority extends beyond death.
Jairus believed Jesus could heal sickness.
Jesus showed He could conquer the grave.
Jairus came seeking one miracle.
He left knowing the Miracle Worker Himself.
And perhaps that is God's deeper purpose in every trial.
Not merely changing our circumstances.
But revealing more of Christ.
The Gospel itself follows this pattern.
On Friday, everything appeared finished.
The disciples scattered.
Hope died.
Darkness covered the land.
The Messiah hung upon a cross.
The scandal seemed complete.
Yet Sunday was coming.
Because God often does His greatest work after people assume the story is over.
The cross became redemption.
The tomb became victory.
Death became life.
Shame became glory.
Scandal became grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is where you are right now.
Waiting.
Grieving.
Praying.
Questioning.
Wondering if Jesus arrived too late.
The lesson from Jairus is simple but life-changing:
Jesus is never late.
He operates beyond human deadlines.
What looks impossible to us remains possible to Him.
What appears dead to us remains under His authority.
What feels finished to us may simply be the place where His glory is about to appear.
If this story spoke to your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What are you trusting Jesus to resurrect in your life?
Your support helps expand the reach of Christ-centered content that points people toward repentance, grace, healing, restoration, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
And remember this:
The same hand that lifted Jairus' daughter is still reaching into impossible situations today.
When everyone else sees an ending, Jesus sees the first sentence of a new chapter.
